newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: Sri Lanka stocks rise on new political optimism.
newsitem.headline: Sri Lanka stocks rise on new political optimism.

text.p: Sri Lankan stocks have shaken off last year's lethargy thanks largely to perceived political stability and central bank moves to buoy the market, analysts said on Thuraday.
The Colombo Stock Exchange's all share index has risen 10.9 percent, or 69.3 points, in April alone. On Thursday, the index ended at 706.8, up 17.71 points on the previous session.

The index rose a paltry five percent in the first three months of 1997. Last year, it fell nine percent as power outages and renewed fighting between the government troops and the Liberation Tiges of Tamil Eelam (LTTE) rebels dulled sentiment.
"The sharp gain in April is due to improved sentiment after investors realised the significance of what had taken place," said Nanda Nair, research director at brokerage John Keells.

A cut in reserve ratios, easing of interest rates, a sweeping election victory by the ruling People's Alliance in local polls held last month and its agreement with the main opposition party to work together to stop the ethnic crisis had brought optimism back to market, he said.
The central bank has cut reserve ratios twice this year to bring the rate down to 12 from 15 percent in a bid to improve money supply and reduce the cost of corporate borrowing.
The benchmark 12-month Treasury Bill was yielding 12.87 percent on Wednesday, compared to a high of 19.2 percent in January 1996.
"Easing fixed-income interest rates serves as a huge incentive to bring institutional investors into equities," said Derendra Abayaratna, fund manager of The Unit Trust Management Co.

The People's Alliance coalition and the main opposition United Natinal Party (UNP) signed an agreement earlier this month to take a bipartisan approach to solve the country's 13-year ethnic conflict, where Tamil rebels are fighting for a separate homeland in the north and east.

"The mere signing of an agreement will not usher in instant peace," said Sanjeeva Gunewardena of Ceylinco Stock Brokers. "But it makes a solution more possible to a conflict which costs the country over five percent of its GDP (gross domestic product)".

While some analysts said the current bullishness called for an upward revision of forecasts for the all share index, others said profit-taking and an evaporation of sentiment would bring the market back to a more sustainable level of growth.
"We will look at an upward revision of the all share (index) from our original year-end forecast of 725 points," said Avanka Herath, an analyst at brokerage Jardine Fleming.
Brokerage John Keells said it was revising to 800 from 725 points its year-end forecast.

The two firms said a revision was justified by the alliance's March election victory and the agreement with the opposition. In addition, low-cost corporate debt was likely to boost company profits and low interest rates would attract investors to the stock market.
But Channa Kurukulasuriya, head of research at brokerage Lanka Securities, was more sanguine.
"The current movement is driven by emotions and we see no significant improvements in sectors which have a big impact on the index," he said.

The banking and finance sector, which accounts for 29 percent of Colombo's market capitalisation of 123.9 billion rupees, had gained only one percent this year, while the manaufacturing sector, which accounts for 15 percent of market capitalisation, had risen only 15 percent, he said.
